clue.text: Pile up tins for fish-eaters

indicators.note: something turned up or stirred up is disturbed, so these letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
tins and cans are the same food containers

explanation.surface: Someone stacks tins of food for creatures that live on fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pile up' reads as one verb, but 'up' alone stirs the four letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelicans are large water birds that scoop fish from the sea in their throat pouches.

clue.text: Sanctimonious, good and holy man with yen for filthy place

blocks.note: PI is informal for pious or sanctimonious
G is the abbreviation for good
ST, saint, is a holy man
Y is the symbol for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: A self-righteous holy man trades money for somewhere dirty, a satire on hypocrisy.
explanation.walkthrough: PI as slang for sanctimonious is a crossword staple; 'and' and 'with' simply add the next pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A sty where pigs are kept is the proverbial example of a dirty, messy room or dwelling.

clue.text: In France, the dessert one threw up, being sick

indicators.note: in a down entry, something thrown up is sent upward, so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: la is French for the
pud is British slang for pudding, a dessert
the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A diner in France vomited a pudding because they were ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Threw up' looks like the sickness itself but is the instruction to turn the pieces over; 'being sick' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To be laid up is to be confined to bed through illness, an idiom for being unwell.

clue.text: Press relayed eerie fact

indicators.note: something relayed is laid again, put down a second time in a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Journalists passed on a spooky piece of news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like the newspapers that relay the fact, but it is a coffee press.
explanation.definitionFit: A cafetière is a plunger coffee maker, called a French press in many countries.

clue.text: He can't go on only ordering creation of tiny things

indicators.note: ordering means arranging, putting the letters into a new sequence

blocks.note: every letter of these words, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A man who cannot carry on keeps ordering things to be made small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordering' reads like placing orders for goods; it tells you to rearrange all fourteen letters of the opening phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Nanotechnology is engineering at the scale of single molecules, building devices far too small to see.

clue.text: Biblical figure suppressed by vilest Herod

indicators.note: what is suppressed is held down inside something else, kept out of view within it

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A figure from scripture is crushed by the wicked King Herod.
explanation.walkthrough: Herod and Esther both being biblical makes the surface plausible; the name sits across the join of 'vilest' and 'Herod'.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is the Jewish queen of Persia whose story is told in the Old Testament book named after her.

clue.text: South of Iowa's capital city

blocks.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
taken as written
IA is the US postal code for Iowa; the possessive ending just links

explanation.surface: It asks for a city lying south of the main city of Iowa.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sends you looking at a map of the American Midwest, but the answer is in the Balkans; 'of' is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Sofia is the capital of Bulgaria, so it is an example of a national capital.

clue.text: £1,000 sheds to become modern way of working

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun, the shared desks used in this working practice; it can also be read as the verb, as in 'she hot-desks'

indicators.note: to become is to change into something else, so the letters turn into a new form

blocks.note: a thousand pounds is a grand, K
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Spending a thousand pounds on garden sheds turns them into offices for a new style of work.
explanation.walkthrough: K for a thousand, from kilo, is standard; 'to' is part of the letters, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot-desking means staff have no fixed desk and take whichever free workstation is available, a recent office practice.

clue.text: Research Yeats. Puzzling? Don't worry!

indicators.note: something puzzling is confused and muddled, so these letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: RES is the standard abbreviation for research
the poet's name, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A student studying a baffling Irish poet is reassured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puzzling' looks like a comment on the poet, but it scrambles his name; Yeats is the Irish poet W. B. Yeats.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to rest easy is an idiom urging them to relax and stop being anxious.

clue.text: Grew ponytail to supply admission of error

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, meaning flexibly, so the letters bend into a new shape

blocks.note: all fourteen letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone grew a ponytail as a way of saying sorry for a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like the verb to provide, but read as 'supple-ly' it means flexibly; 'to' belongs to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A written apology is a formal letter acknowledging a mistake, so it is an admission of having been wrong.

clue.text: Grotesque raptor in fantasy; fierce: I'm nervous, primarily!

definitions.text: Grotesque raptor in fantasy; fierce: I'm nervous, primarily!

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of each word counts

blocks.clueFragment: Grotesque raptor in fantasy; fierce: I'm nervous
blocks.note: the initial letters of these seven words

explanation.surface: A frightened onlooker describes a monstrous bird of prey from legend.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: its initials spell the answer and, read whole, it describes the creature and the fear it causes.
explanation.definitionFit: The griffin of myth has an eagle's head and wings on a lion's body, a fearsome hybrid predator.

clue.text: Denies time for the good in shelters

indicators.note: one thing given for another is a swap, the first taking the second's place

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
G is the abbreviation for good
refuges are places of shelter

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to give the virtuous any time inside places of refuge.
explanation.walkthrough: In REFUGES the G becomes a T; 'in' just locates the swap within the shelters.
explanation.definitionFit: To refute a claim is to argue that it is false, so it is a synonym for contradicting or denying.

clue.text: Faith's tied up, we're told

indicators.note: what we are told reaches us by ear, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: trussed means bound or tied up

explanation.surface: Someone's religious belief is said to be bound up and restricted.
explanation.walkthrough: Faith reads as a woman's name, but it is the definition, and the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trust and faith are synonyms for confident belief in someone or something.

clue.text: Four notes describing a meeting

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round something, so these letters go round another

blocks.note: te, the seventh sol-fa note, four times over
taken as written

explanation.surface: A short musical phrase is used to portray people gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' looks like a link but means drawing round, as a compass describes a circle; the 'a' is a letter, not part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tête-à-tête is a private conversation between two people, literally head to head in French.

clue.text: 21st book of O.T.: timeless casket displayed food containing fruit

indicators.note: less means without, so the abbreviation for time is taken away
things displayed are laid out and arranged afresh, so the letters change order

blocks.note: Eccles is the short form of Ecclesiastes, the twenty-first Old Testament book
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Bible reference and a casket put on show sound like a museum exhibit, ending in something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: CASKET loses its T before rearranging. Eccles cakes are round flaky pastries filled with currants, named after a town near Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: An Eccles cake is a pastry filled with currants, dried fruit, so it is food with fruit inside.

clue.text: Poet going north: 'Say, frightful water in Scotland, mostly'

indicators.note: in a down entry, travelling north means moving upward, so the letters read bottom to top
mostly means not all of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: EG, for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
dire means dreadful or frightful
a loch is a Scottish lake

explanation.surface: A poet travelling up to Scotland remarks on a terrible stretch of water.
explanation.walkthrough: LOCH loses its H, then the whole string of pieces is read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was the English Romantic poet who wrote The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

clue.text: In manner of a member of parliament?

definitions.text: In manner of a member of parliament?

blocks.note: surface reading: behaving like an elected politician
setter's reading: a parliament is the collective noun for a group of owls, so a member is one bird

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the trick: parliament is not Westminster but the collective noun for the birds.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb describes acting like the bird, with a wise or solemn look, as one of that flock would.

clue.text: New Saab assigned to Observer staff, recognizing good work?

indicators.note: something new is remade, so the car's letters come out in a fresh order

blocks.note: the Swedish car make, to be rearranged
a task assigned to someone is on them
Everyman appears in The Observer, a British Sunday newspaper, so its staff call themselves us

explanation.surface: A newspaper hands its staff a new company car as a reward for their efforts.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example, hence the question mark: something given for good work comes as a bonus.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonus is an extra payment given to reward good performance, so receiving something this way recognises effort.

clue.text: Herod's legacy depicted in film with a couple of lines

blocks.note: a western is a cowboy film
W is short for with
taken as written
L stands for line, so two lines are LL

explanation.surface: A movie about King Herod's heritage contains a pair of written lines.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'a' in the clue belongs to 'a couple of lines'; the first stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The Western Wall in Jerusalem is part of the retaining wall Herod built round the Temple Mount, a surviving monument of his reign.

clue.text: Mist up oriel, a little haze

indicators.note: a little of something is only a small part of it, a piece taken from inside

blocks.note: runs from the end of the first word through the second into the third

explanation.surface: A bay window steams up, slightly obscured by condensation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' looks like part of the instruction, but it is simply part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed state of near-unconsciousness, a mental fog or haze.

clue.text: 'Dessert', Canadian native's announced

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out to listeners, so its sound is what matters

blocks.note: the moose is a large deer native to Canada

explanation.surface: A quoted menu item is said to be the speech of an indigenous Canadian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canadian native' suggests a person, but it is an animal; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mousse is a light, airy sweet dish made with whipped cream or egg whites, eaten at the end of a meal.

clue.text: Everyman's run into lav: behold, Everyman's in a muddle

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it, enclosed by it
being in something means sitting inside it, surrounded on both sides

blocks.note: the setter Everyman is I, and 'Everyman is' is I'M
bog is British slang for a lavatory
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run
lo is an old word for look or behold
the setter refers to himself as Everyman, so I; the following 's means is

explanation.surface: The setter dashes into the toilet, announces his arrival and admits to being in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the setter's name, so it gives I; the first 'Everyman's' is 'I am', and in the second the 's is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An imbroglio is a confused, complicated situation, an Italian loanword for a tangle or mess.

clue.text: Advisory board where some participants are late?

definitions.text: Advisory board where some participants are late?

blocks.note: surface reading: a committee giving advice, some of whose members turn up behind time
setter's reading: the late are the dead, and a lettered board lets the departed give advice at a seance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' means dead, not tardy, and the board is a physical board, not a committee.
explanation.definitionFit: The board printed with letters and yes and no is used at seances, supposedly to receive messages from spirits.

clue.text: Trainspotter ultimately missing mass transport system with old-school charm

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so just the final letter is used
what is missing has gone, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: the final letter of this word
a metro is an urban rail network
m is the symbol for mass in physics

explanation.surface: A railway enthusiast misses a vintage train service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trainspotter' looks like the subject of the sentence, but only its tail is used; the underground railway then drops the physics symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Retro describes a style that deliberately imitates fashions of the past, so it has nostalgic, old-fashioned appeal.

clue.text: Smelling what goose produces

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for giving off a strong, unpleasant odour
second meaning: the loud call the bird makes

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'honking' means stinking; the surface suggests a smelly goose.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective is informal British for foul-smelling, and the noun is the harsh trumpeting cry that geese make.

clue.text: Dictionary, American, minimal cash invested – a tragedy

indicators.note: money invested is put inside something, so this piece goes in between the others

blocks.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
US stands for American
1p, one penny, is the smallest sum, with the 1 read as I

explanation.surface: A US dictionary publisher put almost no money in and the result was a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: '1p' is written with the digit one, which the setter treats as the letter I; p is a British penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Oedipus Rex is the ancient Greek tragedy by Sophocles, often shortened to the hero's name.

clue.text: Voyeur, dismal fiancé – essentially, a creep

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so the centre of each word is kept

blocks.note: the central pair of letters
the central pair of letters
the central pair of letters

explanation.surface: A miserable fiancé who spies on people is described as a creepy type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creep' suggests the voyeur, but here it means a toady; each word gives its central two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A creep in British use is also a sycophant, and a yes-man agrees with superiors to win favour.

clue.text: Where Charlotte's often seen to be fancy

blocks.note: first meaning: Princess Charlotte is often pictured beside her brother Prince George
second meaning: an exclamation of surprise, as in 'Fancy that!'

explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte and George are the elder children of Britain's Prince William, photographed together at royal events.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dated British exclamations expressing surprise, used in place of a stronger oath.
